title: Ha'azinu: ask your father (Deuteronomy 32:7)
hook: remember the days of old; ask your father and your elders
tomorrow: Ha'azinu: the eagle over its nest (Deuteronomy 32:11)

segments.voice: Yesterday, tzur, the Rock. Your line was the rock. Today, the song tells you where to go for answers.

A woman sits at her grandmother's funeral, and the questions start to arrive. Not about what was said. About what was never asked. How did you two meet? What was your own grandfather like? What was the hardest year of your life? The answers went with her. In the middle of Ha'azinu, between the Rock and the history of the people, Moses' song gives an instruction aimed at exactly that loss.
screen: `AFTER THE FUNERAL.` → `THE QUESTIONS NEVER ASKED.` → `THE SONG'S INSTRUCTION.`

segments.voice: "Remember the days of old, Consider the years of many generations; Ask thy father, and he will declare unto thee, Thine elders, and they will tell thee." Two pairs. Remember and consider: work you do inside your own head. Ask and be told: work that needs another person. The verse doesn't trust memory alone. You have to go and ask. Father and elders form a kind of ladder. Your father knows his own years. The elders reach further back. And Jewish tradition is built like that ladder. The tractate Pirkei Avot opens with a chain: Moses received the Torah at Sinai and handed it to Joshua, Joshua to the elders, the elders to the prophets, the prophets to the men of the Great Assembly. Each link asked, and was told. The Passover seder runs on asking too. The night is shaped around a child's questions. Notice where the verse puts the responsibility. On the younger one. Ask. The elders' part is to declare and to tell, but they can only answer what someone thinks to ask. Some old people carry stories no one has ever asked for. Some families have one person who knows where everyone came from, and limited time to tell it. The song puts it plainly: memory isn't only kept. It has to be asked for.
screen: `REMEMBER, CONSIDER, ASK.` · `A LADDER OF GENERATIONS.` · `MOSES TO JOSHUA TO THE ELDERS.` · `THE YOUNGER ONE ASKS.` · then, large: `ASK YOUR ELDERS.`

segments.voice: Think of the oldest person you could reach, a parent, a grandparent, an old neighbor, someone at your congregation, and what you don't know about their life. Choose one question, not a quiz but a door: who taught you to cook, or what do you remember about your own grandparents?
Ha'azinu. Give ear. And in it, a command to ask: ask thy father, thine elders.
Your line: ask your elders. They can only answer what someone thinks to ask. That's day five hundred thirty.

screen: `DAY 530 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: HA'AZINU: THE EAGLE OVER ITS NEST (DEUTERONOMY 32:11).`
